summary: This Experimental document describes Roughtime, a protocol for secure rough time synchronization, even for clients with no idea what time it is. It also defines a format for clients to report inconsistencies they see between timeservers, and discusses the surrounding ecosystem.

eli5.summary: A clock that is not exact but trustworthy, and it catches liars who give the wrong time.

questions: how does roughtime detect lying time servers
subtitle: Signed, rough time from several servers, plus proof when one of them lies.

tldr.problem: Common time protocols such as NTP lack essential security features, and a device that has no idea what time it is cannot validate X.509 certificates to bootstrap secure time.
tldr.mechanism: A client sends a request with a nonce to several servers. Each server signs a response containing a timestamp and a radius, using a Merkle tree to cover many requests with one signature. Chaining responses lets the client prove if a server reported inconsistent times.
tldr.outcome: Clients get authenticated rough time from a fairly static server list and can report misbehaving servers, but the RFC defines only the on-wire protocol and leaves the surrounding ecosystem to experiments.

today: RFC 10049 is an Experimental protocol published in October 2026. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The RFC says operational experience is still needed to judge whether Roughtime is viable for secure time bootstrapping.

sections.title: The Problem Roughtime Solves
sections.content:
Time synchronization is essential to Internet security, yet widely deployed protocols such as NTP (RFC 5905) lack essential security features, and even Network Time Security (RFC 8915) has no way to observe whether servers behave correctly. A client may also have no idea of the time at all, which breaks X.509 certificate validation.

Roughtime aims to give a device a rough idea of the current time from a fairly static configuration: a list of servers and their long-term public keys, which are the roots of trust. It also lets clients report any inconsistencies they observe between servers. Unlike Khronos (RFC 9523), it produces external evidence that servers report incompatible times, which needs a different timestamp format, so it cannot be a mere extension to NTP.

The document is Experimental. It describes only the on-wire protocol, plus the server list and malfeasance report formats. How lists are maintained and distributed, and how accusations are judged, are left out.
sections.eli5: A gadget that just woke up does not know what day it is. Roughtime lets it ask several trusted helpers and keep their signed answers, so it can tell if one helper is fibbing.

sections.title: Single-Server and Multi-Server Modes
sections.content:
At its simplest, Roughtime is a one-round protocol. A fresh client sends a request with a nonce, and the server returns a signed response with a timestamp and a radius saying how certain it is. Because the nonce is included in the signed data, the response could only have been created after the request arrived.

To let one signature cover many clients, the signed value is the root of a Merkle tree whose leaves include the hash of each request. This spreads the cost of signing over a number of requests.

With several servers, a client can detect, prove and report inconsistencies. A server guarantees its timestamp was generated after it received the request and before it sent the response. If its time clashes with other servers, that indicates error or malfeasance. The RFC notes that a review and impeachment process is needed for any real impeachment, and it is out of scope.
sections.eli5: Each helper stamps the note with your secret word, so the note must be newer than your question. One stamp can cover a whole crowd of questions at once.

sections.title: Messages, Tags and Packets
sections.content:
A Roughtime message is a map of (tag, value) pairs. It starts with a header holding the number of pairs N as a uint32, then N-1 offsets, then N tags, followed by the values. Integers are serialized least significant byte first. A tag is four octets: one to four capital ASCII letters followed by zero to three zero octets, so NONC is the uint32 0x434e4f4e. Tags and offsets are sorted in ascending order, and a tag MUST NOT appear twice in a header. Values can themselves be Roughtime messages.

On the wire, a packet is the 64-bit value 0x4d49544847554f52 ("ROUGHTIM" in ASCII), a uint32 length, and then the message. Packets travel as UDP datagrams or over TCP streams, and servers SHOULD support both. A timestamp is a uint64 count of seconds since 1 January 1970, assuming every day has 86400 seconds, so leap seconds have no unambiguous representation.
sections.eli5: Every message is a labelled box of smaller labelled boxes, and every packet starts with the secret word ROUGHTIM so you know what you are holding.

sections.title: Requests and Responses
sections.content:
A request contains the tags VER (supported versions; this document is version 1), NONC (a 32-byte nonce) and TYPE (0 in requests). It SHOULD include SRV, which names the long-term key the client expects. Over UDP the request SHOULD be at least 1024 bytes, padded with the all-zero ZZZZ tag, and servers MUST NOT send responses larger than the request, which prevents amplification attacks.

A response has SIG, NONC, TYPE (1), PATH, SREP, CERT and INDX. SREP holds the signed content: the chosen version, RADI (the accuracy in seconds, which MUST NOT be zero), MIDP (the timestamp of processing), the server's VERS list and the Merkle ROOT. CERT carries a delegated key (PUBK, valid between MINT and MAXT) signed by the server's long-term key. Signatures are 64-byte Ed25519.

The client rebuilds the Merkle root from its own request using INDX and PATH (up to 32 hashes of 32 bytes each), using the first 32 bytes of SHA-512. A response is valid only if the CERT signature, the MINT to MAXT window, the Merkle proof and the SREP signature all check out. The protocol has no error messages, to avoid the Kiss-o'-Death weakness that NTP has.
sections.eli5: You send a question with a secret word. The reply carries the time, how unsure the clock is, and a proof that your question was in the batch it signed. You check every stamp before you trust it.

sections.title: How Clients Catch Cheating Servers
sections.content:
A client needs a list of servers, at least three of them operational and not run by the same parties. It randomly picks at least three and queries them in sequence, twice, in the same order. The first nonce is random. Each later nonce is H(resp || rand), built from the entire previous response and a fresh 32-byte random value, which chains the responses together.

For each pair of responses (i, j) with i received first, the client MUST check that MIDP_i - RADI_i is at most MIDP_j + RADI_j. If any response fails this causal ordering, there has been malfeasance, and the client SHOULD generate a report, alert the user and measure again.

A malfeasance report is a JSON object with a list of responses, each holding base64 values for rand, publicKey, request and response. It is POSTed over HTTPS to the URL in the server list, with exponential backoff. Clients MUST NOT report signature failures or other protocol errors. Clients also retry with exponential backoff, and the RFC recommends an initial 1 second interval, a base of 1.5 and a 24 hour maximum.
sections.eli5: You ask the helpers one after another, and each question includes a copy of the last answer. If the times cannot fit together in order, you have signed proof that someone lied.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
Roughtime gives no confidentiality, which the RFC calls a minor impact given the nature of timestamps. Integrity and authenticity cover only data inside SREP, so new tags SHOULD be added there. Private keys MUST be generated as described in Section 5.1.5 of RFC 8032.

If a delegated private key leaks, even after MAXT, it could sign invalid times in its MINT to MAXT range. Querying multiple servers protects against that. Ed25519 is not quantum resistant, so this version will not survive quantum computers and a later version will be needed.

On privacy, the protocol is designed to obscure client identifiers, but generating nonces in a nonrandom way can leak private data or let clients be tracked between networks. To discourage ossification, servers SHOULD sometimes send deliberately flawed responses (grease), and clients MUST reject invalid ones.
sections.eli5: Anyone can see the time you asked for, but nobody can fake the signed answer. Using several helpers means one stolen stamp is not enough to fool you.
